blocks.p: On a bike you feel a headwind even on a calm day. A boat is the same: the sails get the true wind plus the wind from the boat’s own speed – the apparent wind. The faster the boat, the further forward it moves.

Sailing straight into the wind is impossible: about 40–45° either side is the “no-go zone”. So an SSL47 zigzags upwind (close-hauled) and also sails angles downwind – a broad reach is faster than dead downwind.
In a tack the bow turns through the wind, in a gybe the stern. Every manoeuvre costs speed – clean tacks and gybes gain metres.
Known since the 2016 Olympics for shifty, gusty wind and current at the narrow entrance. In the afternoon the sea breeze often builds. Whoever catches the shifts and gusts first wins.

quiz.q: Why does a sailing boat zigzag upwind?
a: It can’t sail straight into the wind
quiz.e: Inside the no-go zone (about 40–45° each side) the sails produce no drive.

a: True wind plus the wind from the boat’s speed
quiz.e: The sails feel the sum of the true wind and the boat-speed wind.

blocks.p: When two boats on opposite tacks cross, the boat on port tack (wind from the left) keeps clear. Typical scene: the port boat ducks behind the other’s stern.
When two boats on the same tack overlap, the windward boat (closer to the wind) keeps clear of the leeward boat.
Without an overlap, the boat clear astern keeps clear of the boat clear ahead.
From the moment the bow passes head to wind until the boat is close-hauled again, it must keep clear of everyone. A tack too close in front of a rival means a penalty.
It can’t do anything it likes: it must avoid contact (rule 14), give room to keep clear when changing course (rule 16) and give room when it has just gained right of way (rule 15).

quiz.q: Two boats cross. Boat A has the wind from the right, boat B from the left. Who keeps clear?
quiz.e: B is on port tack (wind from the left) and must keep clear of starboard boat A – rule 10.

quiz.q: Two boats overlap on the same tack. Who keeps clear?
quiz.e: Rule 11: windward keeps clear of leeward.

quiz.q: A boat tacks right in front of another. Who must keep clear during the tack?
quiz.e: Rule 13: until it is close-hauled again, the tacking boat keeps clear.

quiz.q: May a right-of-way boat deliberately stay on a collision course?
a: Yes, it has right of way
quiz.e: Rule 14 applies to every boat – including the one with right of way.

chapters.sub: The SSL47 and who does what

blocks.p: A simplified RC44 without electronics, about 13.4 m long, with a heavy keel, bowsprit and coffee-grinder winches. All teams sail identical, supplied boats – only the crew makes the difference.

From back to front: helm and tactician at the stern, main trimmer on the mainsail, two trimmers on jib and gennaker, grinder on the pedestal, pit in the middle, mid-bow at the mast and bow right at the front. Crews are mixed: at least two people of the other gender on board.
Upwind the boat sails with mainsail and jib (a smaller, heavy jib in strong wind), downwind with the big gennaker on the bowsprit.

quiz.q: Who decides which side of the course the boat goes?
quiz.e: The tactician reads wind and rivals and calls the route.

quiz.q: Who signals the distance to the start line by hand?
quiz.e: The bow has the best view of the line.

blocks.p: Standard under rule 26: 5 minutes warning (class flag), 4 minutes preparatory (e.g. flag P), 1 minute (preparatory flag down), start (class flag down). Flags count, not sounds.
The start is between the committee boat and the pin. The aim: full speed exactly on the gun – not early. Before the start boats stalk each other in dial-ups and circles like in match racing.
A boat over the line at the gun (OCS) is recalled with flag X and has to go back. The first substitute means a general recall – everyone starts again.

quiz.q: What does flag X after the start mean?
a: Individual recall – at least one boat was early
quiz.e: X = individual recall. The boat involved must return behind the line.

quiz.q: Sound and flag don’t match in the start sequence. What counts?
quiz.e: The flag signals are what count.

blocks.p: The boats sail a windward–leeward course: start, up to the windward mark, set the gennaker, down to the leeward gate, up again – with an offset mark and finish variant as instructed.

A circle of three boat lengths lies around every mark. What counts is the moment the first boat reaches the zone: whoever is overlapped inside then gets room to round the mark. Most protests happen right here.

quiz.q: How big is the zone around a mark?
quiz.e: Three hull lengths of the nearer boat (two in match racing).

quiz.q: When is it decided who gets mark-room?
a: When the first boat reaches the zone
quiz.e: Rule 18.2: what counts is the moment the first boat reaches the zone.

chapters.sub: Decided on the water, right away

blocks.p: Racing follows Appendix UF: umpires follow right behind the boats. A boat protests with yellow flag Y and the umpires decide at once – green-white means no penalty, red means penalty, black means disqualification.
A penalised boat must sail a penalty manoeuvre straight away and usually loses places. Under Appendix UF the default is one turn. The exact form used in Rio is in the sailing instructions.

quiz.q: The umpire shows a red flag. What does it mean?
quiz.e: Red = penalty, green-white = no penalty, black = disqualification.

blocks.p: Each round is sailed in groups of four, one race per group per day. The top two of each group go through. Formally it is fleet racing, tactically it often feels like a match race: you control your direct rival for second place.
First place scores 4 points, fourth place one. On the last day of each round the race counts double (8-6-4-2) – so everything can still change at the end.
1/32 finals (19–22 Nov), 1/16 finals (26–29 Nov), 1/8 finals (2–5 Dec), quarter-finals (7–10 Dec), semi-finals (12 Dec) and the final on 13 December. Higher-ranked nations join later.

quiz.q: How many points does the winner get on the last day of a round?
How many boats per group go through?
quiz.e: The top two of each group of four.

glossary.d: Steers the boat from the back. Turns the tactician’s calls into course and speed and drives the starts and manoeuvres.
Reads wind, current and rivals and makes the calls: which side of the course, when to tack, whom to cover. Tells the helm what to do.
Trims the mainsail with sheet, traveller and backstay – the key tool for speed, pointing and controlling heel in gusts.
Trims jib and gennaker. Keeps the jib spot-on upwind and the gennaker “just on the edge of curling” downwind.
Powers the pedestal winch (coffee grinder) that winds in sheets and halyards – above all in tacks, gybes and gennaker sets.
Runs the halyards and control lines in the middle of the boat: sails up and down, cunningham, outhaul. Links bow and back of the boat in manoeuvres.
Works between bow and mast: helps set and drop the gennaker, pulls sails into the hatch and backs up the bow.
Right at the front: signals the distance to the start line by hand, prepares gennaker and bowsprit and works every mark rounding.
Team utility player: covers several positions and comes in depending on wind and the crew weight limit.
Sporting leader of the national team. Often – not always – the helm or tactician on board.
The Gold Cup one-design: a simplified RC44 without electronics, about 13.4 m long. All teams sail identical, supplied boats.
The big sail behind the mast, attached to the boom.
Headsail for upwind legs. In strong wind the crew switches to a smaller, heavy jib.
Large, full downwind sail flown from the bowsprit – the colourful sail on the downwind legs.
Retractable pole at the bow on which the gennaker is flown.
Fin with a heavy lead bulb under the hull: stops the boat sliding sideways and keeps it upright.
Blade at the stern used to steer.
Horizontal spar on the mast that holds the foot of the mainsail.
Line used to pull a sail in or ease it out.
Line that hoists a sail.
Pulls the mast aft. Tight = flatter sails, less power – the main tool to depower.
Track across the cockpit that moves the boom sideways without changing the sail’s shape.
Drum the sheets are wrapped around. On the SSL47 driven by the grinders via a pedestal.
Small ribbons on the sail that show whether the airflow is clean.
The bow turns through the wind and the boat changes from one tack to the other. Typical upwind.
The stern turns through the wind; main and gennaker swap sides. Typical downwind – tricky in strong wind.
Turn more towards the wind.
Turn away from the wind.
Pulling the gennaker up at the windward mark – bow, mid-bow and pit work together.
Taking the gennaker down before the leeward mark. Late or messy costs places.
The boat spins uncontrollably into the wind and heels hard – usually under gennaker in a gust.
Before the start two boats turn head to wind side by side and stalk each other – match-race tactics.
Tacking just ahead and to leeward of a rival: their wind is disturbed and they usually have to tack away.
The leader stays between the rival and the mark to keep them behind.
The wind felt by someone standing still.
True wind plus the wind from the boat’s own speed – what the sails ‘see’. The faster the boat, the further forward it moves.
A change in wind direction. A lift lets you point higher, a header forces you down. Playing shifts wins races.
A short burst of stronger wind, visible as a darker patch on the water.
Disturbed, weaker wind behind and to leeward of another boat.
Thermal wind from sea to land that builds in the afternoon. Called “viração” in Rio.
Moving water that carries the boats. Noticeable at the narrow entrance of Guanabara Bay.
As close to the wind as possible – for the SSL47 roughly 40–45° to the true wind.
Wind straight from the side.
Wind from behind at an angle – the fastest gennaker course.
Wind straight from behind. Fast boats zigzag here too.
From here you can reach the mark without another tack.
How fast you actually make progress towards the target, up- or downwind.
Wind from the right (starboard), boom on the left. Starboard has right of way over port (rule 10).
Wind from the left (port). Must keep clear of boats on starboard.
Windward = the side the wind comes from; leeward = the other side. When overlapped, the windward boat keeps clear (rule 11).
Two boats are overlapped when neither is clear ahead – decisive for right of way and mark-room.
Completely behind a line across the other boat’s stern. Must keep clear (rule 12).
Stay out of the right-of-way boat’s way so it can sail its course without avoiding you.
The right to hold your course. Not unlimited: the right-of-way boat must still avoid contact (rule 14).
Room to sail to the mark, round it and leave it astern. The boat overlapped inside when the zone is reached gets it (rule 18).
Circle three boat lengths around a mark. Who is overlapped inside when the zone is reached gets mark-room.
The course a boat would sail to finish as fast as possible if the others weren’t there.
Imaginary line between the committee boat (right) and the pin end (left).
The left end of the start line, marked by a buoy.
Over the line at the start signal. Recalled with flag X – the boat must go back and restart.
The mark at the top of the course, upwind. Gennaker goes up here.
Two marks at the bottom of the course – each boat chooses which one to round.
Follows the boats in a RIB and decides on the spot with flags: green-white = no penalty, red = penalty.
A boat that sees a foul hails “Protest” and shows yellow flag Y. The umpires decide on the spot.
A penalised boat must sail a penalty manoeuvre and usually loses places. The exact form is in the sailing instructions.
World Sailing’s rules appendix for fleet racing with on-water umpires – the basis of the Gold Cup format.
On the last day of each round the race counts double: 8-6-4-2 instead of 4-3-2-1.
The tall spar that carries mainsail, jib and gennaker. Bent by backstay and sheets to flatten the mainsail in strong wind.
Wire from the bow to the mast that holds the mast forward; the jib is set on it.
The body of the boat. The SSL47’s hull is light and narrow for speed; keel and rudder sit underneath.
Line or ram that pulls the boom down. Keeps the mainsail’s leech under control, above all downwind.
Pulls the front edge of the mainsail down. Tighter = flatter sail with the depth further forward – used as the wind builds.
Stretches the foot of the mainsail along the boom. Eased for power in light wind, pulled tight upwind in a breeze.
Pull a sheet in so the sail sits closer to the boat’s centreline. The opposite is to ease.
Let a sheet out a little. Eased sails are fuller and more powerful – and depower a boat that is overpressed in a gust.
Bear away briefly to pass behind the stern of a boat with right of way instead of tacking.
Turning around a mark. Good roundings are tight and fast, with the next sail already set – boats gain or lose places here.
Judging before the start how many seconds the boat needs to reach the line at full speed – so it crosses exactly at the gun.
Sailing towards the wind in a zigzag (close-hauled). The first leg after the start is upwind.
Sailing away from the wind with the gennaker up. Fast boats sail angles and gybe rather than going straight downwind.
Sailing upwind as close to the wind as possible. Higher pointing gains distance to windward, but costs speed.
Sailing slightly lower than possible to go faster – useful in waves or to escape bad air.
A patch of lighter wind. The opposite of a gust – trimmers ease to keep the boat moving.
One stretch of the course between two marks – upwind or downwind. Rounds and laps are counted in legs.
The race officers’ boat at the right-hand end of the start line. Flags and sound signals for the start are given from here.
Line between a committee boat and a mark. A boat finishes when any part of it crosses the line from the course side.
Five minutes before the start: class flag up with a sound signal. From now on the countdown runs.
Four minutes before the start: flag P, I, Z, U or black. The flag says which start rule applies.
Flag X with one sound right after the start: one or more boats were over early and must come back.
Too many boats over early or unclear: the whole start is called back with the First Substitute flag and two sounds, then restarted.
Strictest start rule: a boat inside the triangle formed by the ends of the start line and the first mark during the last minute is disqualified – even if the start is recalled.
A boat inside the triangle formed by the ends of the start line and the first mark during the last minute is disqualified – unless the race is restarted.
Ranking of the nations built from the SSL points of their sailors. Used for seeding at the Gold Cup.
The decisive stage in Rio: knock-out rounds in groups of four, the top two of each group go through to the next round.
